# Introduction

The other summary statistics of _GenomicBreaks_ were each written to measure
something that has a biological meaning, such as synteny or strand
randomisation.  The twelve _monkey indices_ were not.  They were retained from
a screen of 5,420 candidate functions assembled mechanically ("monkey typing")
from the columns of an alignment table and from generic descriptive
statistics.  A candidate was retained when its value was:

 - reproducible between the alignment of _A_ to _B_ and the alignment of _B_
   to _A_;
 - more alike between genome pairs that share an ancestor than between other
   pairs;
 - different from the value obtained after shuffling the order and the strand
   of the alignments;
 - not strongly correlated with the statistics that already existed, nor with
   the other candidates retained (absolute rank correlation below 0.6).

What the indices mean biologically, if anything, is to be found.  Each one is
named after a famous monkey.

This vignette shows how to compute the indices, defines them, and reports how
they were selected and how they behave on the 1,910 alignments of the screen.
The screen was run on 2026-11-11 by Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic; the R
functions, their tests and this vignette were written in the same session.
The numbers reported here describe the alignments of the screen, and will
differ on other data.

# Computing the indices

Each function takes a `GBreaks` object that was not coalesced, and returns one
number.  No function has a parameter.  We use the alignment of two yeast
genomes that is distributed with the package.

```{r load_yeast}
gb <- load_genomic_breaks(
  system.file("extdata/SacCer3__SacPar.gff3.gz", package = "GenomicBreaks"))
gb
```

Ten functions only use the coordinates and the strand of the alignments.

```{r ten_indices}
monkeys <- list(wukong = wukong_index, abu = abu_index, albert = albert_index,
                marcel = marcel_index, imo = imo_index, rafiki = rafiki_index,
                hanuman = hanuman_index, jack = jack_index, able = able_index,
                mizaru = mizaru_index)
sapply(monkeys, \(f) f(gb))
```

`george_index()` and `baker_index()` also use the alignment score, the number
of alignment columns and the number of gap openings (metadata columns `score`,
`aLength` and `gapOpens`), which `load_genomic_breaks()` provides for files in
_blasttab+_ format.  They stop with an error when a column is missing.  The
GFF3 file of this example records the score only: lower bounds of the two other
columns are used here for illustration.

```{r two_indices}
gb$aLength  <- pmax(width(gb), width(gb$query))
gb$gapOpens <- as.integer(width(gb) != width(gb$query))
c(george = george_index(gb), baker = baker_index(gb))
```

## Representation of the genomes

The values do not depend on the order of the sequences, nor on the orientation
in which each sequence is written: reversing sequences with `reverse()` does
not change them.  The _target_ and the _query_ genomes are not exchangeable:
the values on `swap(gb)` differ, more for some indices than for others.  Note
that `swap()` drops the metadata columns that `george_index()` and
`baker_index()` need.

```{r representation}
gbl <- forceSeqLengths(gb)
rbind(
  loaded          = sapply(monkeys, \(f) f(gbl)),
  reversed_target = sapply(monkeys, \(f) f(reverse(gbl))),
  reversed_query  = sapply(monkeys, \(f) f(reverse(gbl, query = TRUE))),
  swapped         = sapply(monkeys, \(f) f(swap(gbl)))
) |> round(3)
```

## Values that can not be computed

A function returns `NA` when it has fewer than three values to summarise, or
when one of the vectors that it uses does not vary.  This happens with very
few alignments.  It also happens to `jack_index()` and `able_index()` when the
alignments are perfectly colinear, because every rank step is then 1, and to
`mizaru_index()` when fewer than three junctions remain after coalescing.

```{r undefined}
sapply(monkeys, \(f) f(gb[1:2]))
```

The functions stop with an error when ranges are on the `*` strand.

# The twelve functions

| Function | Monkey | What it computes |
|----------------|--------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| `wukong_index()`  | Sun Wukong: the Monkey King of the Chinese novel _Journey to the West_ | Tail weight of the query gaps between consecutive alignments |
| `abu_index()`     | Abu: kleptomaniac pet monkey of the street thief in the _Aladdin_ films | Quartile skewness of the gap contrast (target gap against query gap) |
| `albert_index()`  | Albert II: rhesus macaque, first primate to reach space, in 1949 | Excess kurtosis of the gap contrast |
| `marcel_index()`  | Marcel: white-headed capuchin kept by Ross in the sitcom _Friends_ | Spread of the shift in relative position between the two genomes |
| `imo_index()`     | Imo: Japanese macaque of Koshima who started washing sweet potatoes | Correlation of distance to the sequence end between neighbouring alignments, across genomes |
| `rafiki_index()`  | Rafiki: mandrill shaman who presents the newborn cub in _The Lion King_ | Rank correlation of the query gap with the distance to the query sequence end |
| `hanuman_index()` | Hanuman: monkey-faced Hindu deity, devoted companion of Rama in the _Ramayana_ | Rank correlation of alignment width with the jump in distance to the query sequence end |
| `jack_index()`    | Jack: chacma baboon who operated railway signals in South Africa in the 1880s | Rank correlation of the size of a jump on the query with its direction |
| `able_index()`    | Able: rhesus macaque, Miss Baker's companion on the 1959 spaceflight | Correlation of the size of a jump on the query with the jump in distance to the query sequence end |
| `mizaru_index()`  | Mizaru: the see-no-evil monkey carved at the Toshogu shrine in Nikko | Rank correlation of the target gap between coalesced alignments with the jump in distance to the query sequence end |
| `george_index()`  | Curious George: inquisitive little monkey of the children's books by the Reys | Correlation of the target gap with the score density of the flanking alignments |
| `baker_index()`   | Miss Baker: squirrel monkey who survived a suborbital spaceflight in 1959 | Width-weighted correlation of gap openings per column with the size of the flanking gaps |

The exact definitions are in `?monkey_indices`.

## Terms

All the functions sort the alignments on the _target_ genome.
`mizaru_index()` then coalesces them; the others use them as they are.

 - **Junction**: two consecutive alignments on the same _target_ sequence.
   **Same-query junction**: a junction whose two alignments are also on the
   same _query_ sequence.
 - **Target gap**, **query gap**: number of bases between the two alignments
   of a junction on that genome, plus one.
 - **Gap contrast** of a same-query junction: (_t_ - _q_) / (_t_ + _q_), where
   _t_ and _q_ are its target gap and its query gap.  It is near -1 when the
   two alignments are neighbours on the _target_ and far apart on the _query_.
 - **Rank step**: number of positions between the two alignments in the order
   of the _query_ genome (1 for neighbours).  **Direction**: +1 when they
   follow each other on the _query_ as their common strand implies, -1 in the
   opposite case, 0 when they are on opposite strands.
 - **Edge distance**: distance from the centre of an alignment to the nearest
   end of its sequence, from 0 at the ends to 1 in the middle.  **Relative
   position**: position of the centre, from 0 to 1.
 - **Coalesced alignments**: runs of consecutive colinear alignments merged
   into one, as `coalesce_contigs()` does.  The junctions that remain between
   them are those where colinearity breaks.
 - Sizes (widths, gaps, rank steps) are used on the logarithmic scale.

## Reading of the numbers

The readings follow from the definitions and from the values after shuffling;
they are not biological interpretations.  The observed values are medians of
the clades of the screen (see [Behaviour on the alignments of the screen]).

`wukong_index()`

:   Tail weight of the query gaps: range between the 10th and the 90th
    percentiles, divided by the interquartile range.  A log-normal
    distribution gives 1.90; heavier tails give more.  Observed: 1.3 in the
    molluscs and Pezizomycotina, 1.9 to 2.0 in insects and fishes, 2.6 to 3.3
    in Rickettsiales, Nanobdellati and Deinococcota.

`abu_index()`

:   Quartile skewness of the gap contrast.  Near 0 when the gaps of most
    junctions are similar on the two genomes; negative when a quarter to a
    half of the junctions have a much wider query gap; towards +1 when more
    than half have.  Observed: within 0.06 of 0 in insects, fishes, Primates,
    Gastropoda, Buchnera and Saccharomycotina; -0.10 in Discoba, -0.16 in
    Bivalvia; 0.52 to 0.91 in the other bacteria, Nanobdellati and
    Pezizomycotina.  This reading was checked on 182 alignments: the median
    is 0.04, -0.08, -0.18, 0.68 and 0.68 when the share of junctions with a
    contrast below -0.5 is under 10 %, 10 to 25 %, 25 to 50 %, 50 to 75 % and
    over 75 %.

`albert_index()`

:   Excess kurtosis of the gap contrast.  Negative when the contrasts spread
    between -1 and 1; high when nearly all sit at one value.  Observed: -1.4
    in Primates, -1.1 to 0.6 in the other eukaryotes, 1.8 to 10.7 in the
    bacteria other than Buchnera and in Nanobdellati.  156 after shuffling.

`marcel_index()`

:   Standard deviation of the shift in relative position between the genomes.
    0 when every alignment is at the same relative position on both; 0.236
    when the two positions are independent.  Observed: 0.007 in Buchnera,
    0.21 to 0.24 in every other clade; 0.17 for pairs with a P distance below
    0.05.

`imo_index()`

:   Correlation between the edge distance of an alignment on the _target_ and
    that of its neighbours on the _query_.  1 when the distance to the
    sequence end is kept, 0 when it is not.  Observed: 0.995 in Buchnera; 0.22
    to 0.31 in Eupercaria, Ovalentaria and Primates; 0.09 in
    Other_Neoteleostei; 0.04 or less elsewhere.  0.76 for pairs with a P
    distance below 0.05, 0.03 or less above 0.25.

`rafiki_index()`

:   Rank correlation of the query gap with the mean edge distance on the
    _query_.  -0.33 after shuffling, for a geometric reason: two alignments
    that are far apart can not both be in the middle of the sequence.
    Observed: -0.17 to -0.29 in the bacteria other than Buchnera and in
    Nanobdellati; -0.08 to 0.04 elsewhere.  Mostly a property of the _query_
    genome (symmetry 0.08).

`hanuman_index()`

:   Rank correlation of the mean width of two consecutive alignments with the
    jump in edge distance on the _query_.  Between colinear neighbours the
    jump is the distance between their centres, which grows with their
    widths: positive values.  Elsewhere the jump is unrelated to the widths:
    0.  Observed: 0.77 in Buchnera; 0.24 to 0.32 in Eupercaria, Primates and
    Bivalvia; 0.18 or less elsewhere, about 0 in the other prokaryotes.

`jack_index()`

:   Rank correlation of the rank step with the direction.  Negative when the
    long steps are those that go against the strand.  0 after shuffling.
    Observed: -0.70 and -0.72 in the two mollusc clades, -0.21 in
    Rickettsiales, -0.27 to -0.59 elsewhere.  Undefined for 89 alignments, 82
    of them in Buchnera, where steps or directions do not vary.

`able_index()`

:   Correlation, over same-query junctions, of the rank step with the jump in
    edge distance on the _query_.  Positive when the junctions that jump
    furthest in the order of the _query_ are also those where the distance to
    the sequence end changes most.  0.45 after shuffling: alignments close in
    the _query_ order are close on the sequence, so their edge distances are
    alike.  Observed: 0.94 in Buchnera, over the 50 alignments where it is
    defined; 0.57 to 0.67 in the other bacteria and Nanobdellati; 0.72 in
    Discoba; 0.76 to 0.82 in the other eukaryotes.  Undefined for 87
    alignments, 82 of them in Buchnera, where the rank steps do not vary.

`mizaru_index()`

:   Rank correlation, over the junctions between coalesced alignments, of the
    target gap with the jump in edge distance on the _query_.  Positive when
    the widest target gaps lie between coalesced alignments whose distances to
    the _query_ sequence end differ most.  0 after shuffling.  Observed: 0.31
    in Apoidea; -0.03 to 0.09 in the other clades except Buchnera.  In
    Buchnera, -0.15 over the 50 alignments that have at least three such
    junctions, with quartiles at -0.60 and 0.29.  Undefined for 83
    alignments, 82 of them in Buchnera.

`george_index()`

:   Correlation of the target gap with the mean score per alignment column of
    the two flanking alignments.  Negative when wide gaps lie between
    low-scoring alignments.  0 after shuffling.  Observed: -0.28 in the two
    mollusc clades; -0.10 to -0.15 in fishes, Primates, Pezizomycotina and
    Buchnera; -0.01 to -0.08 elsewhere.

`baker_index()`

:   Correlation, weighted by alignment width, of the gap openings per
    alignment column with the size of the flanking target gaps.  Positive
    when alignments with many gap openings lie next to wide gaps.  0 after
    shuffling.  Observed: 0.16 and 0.17 in the two mollusc clades; 0.07 and
    0.09 in Eupercaria and Primates; -0.06 in Buchnera; within 0.05 of 0
    elsewhere.

## Metrics in the screen

```{r metrics, echo=FALSE}
f <- read.delim("MonkeyIndices_functions.tsv")
dec <- function(x, digits = 3) {
  x[abs(x) < 0.5 * 10^-digits] <- 0
  ifelse(abs(x) >= 10, sprintf("%.0f", x), sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), x))
}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    paste0("`", f$fun, "()`"), dec(f$median), dec(f$shuffled),
    sprintf("%.1f %%", 100 * f$departs), dec(f$reciprocal, 2), dec(f$symmetry, 2),
    paste0(f$closest_label, ": ", dec(f$closest_r, 2)), dec(f$others_r, 2)),
  col.names = c("Function", "Median", "Shuffled", "Departs", "Reciprocal",
                "Symmetry", "Closest existing statistic", "Others"),
  align = "lrrrrrlr")
```

 - **Median**, **Shuffled**: median of the function over one alignment of each
   of the 955 genome pairs of the screen, and median after shuffling these
   alignments.
 - **Departs**: share of the genome pairs in which the value differs from 5
   shuffles by at least 3 standard deviations.
 - **Reciprocal**: rank correlation between the value on the alignment of _A_
   to _B_ and the value on the alignment of _B_ to _A_ after exchanging
   _target_ and _query_ (median of the 16 clades).
 - **Symmetry**: rank correlation between the values on the two alignments
   without exchanging _target_ and _query_: near 1 for a property of the pair
   of genomes, near 0 for a property of the _target_ genome.
 - **Closest existing statistic**: largest absolute rank correlation with any
   of 192 reference statistics, over four ways to compute it: on all
   alignments or within clades, and each also after removing the P distance.
 - **Others**: largest absolute rank correlation with another monkey index,
   computed in the same ways.

# The screen

## Alignments

The screen used 1,910 alignments: 955 genome pairs in both orders, from 182
genomes of 16 clades of the project _Scrambling in the Tree of Life_, 156.8
million alignment blocks in total.  In each clade, the script
`extractMonkeySubset.py` computed the P distance of every ordered pair of
genomes (proportion of the aligned bases that differ, as in `P_distance()`),
built a UPGMA tree, cut it in two, and picked 12 genomes when possible so
that the selection contains close, intermediate and distant pairs.

| Clade | Seed | Genomes | Alignments | Median blocks per alignment | P, minimum | P, median | P, maximum |
|-------|------|--------:|-----------:|----------------------------:|-----------:|----------:|-----------:|
| Buchnera           | MAM8 | 12 | 132 |     142 | 0.002 | 0.331 | 0.360 |
| Deinococcota       | MAM8 | 12 | 132 |     911 | 0.006 | 0.396 | 0.420 |
| Nanobdellati       | MAM8 |  9 |  72 |     142 | 0.242 | 0.480 | 0.537 |
| Neisseriales       | MAM8 | 12 | 132 |     758 | 0.004 | 0.397 | 0.474 |
| Pezizomycotina     | MAM8 |  9 |  72 |   5,441 | 0.003 | 0.386 | 0.403 |
| Rickettsiales      | MAM8 | 12 | 132 |     353 | 0.007 | 0.427 | 0.461 |
| Saccharomycotina   | MAM8 | 12 | 132 |   2,664 | 0.003 | 0.412 | 0.434 |
| Apoidea            | RY4  | 12 | 132 |  72,091 | 0.003 | 0.215 | 0.230 |
| Bivalvia           | RY4  | 12 | 132 |  10,388 | 0.019 | 0.354 | 0.424 |
| Discoba            | RY4  | 12 | 132 |     311 | 0.004 | 0.413 | 0.473 |
| Eupercaria         | RY4  | 12 | 132 | 164,986 | 0.005 | 0.199 | 0.229 |
| Gastropoda         | RY4  | 12 | 132 |   6,459 | 0.019 | 0.307 | 0.442 |
| Other_Neoteleostei | RY4  | 11 | 110 | 118,600 | 0.003 | 0.222 | 0.245 |
| Otomorpha          | RY4  | 12 | 132 | 104,504 | 0.011 | 0.228 | 0.266 |
| Ovalentaria        | RY4  | 12 | 132 | 184,655 | 0.002 | 0.217 | 0.246 |
| Primates           | RY4  |  9 |  72 | 926,489 | 0.002 | 0.186 | 0.222 |

The seed is the seeding scheme given to the aligner (LAST).  Most pairs are
distant: the median P distance is 0.33, and 84 alignments (4 %) have a P
distance below 0.1.  Close pairs are therefore few in every test below.

The existing statistics were represented by 192 reference columns per
alignment:

 - 156 values from the YAML files of the statistics pipeline of the project;
 - 9 values of package functions absent from these files (karyotype index,
   tau index, totals of the breakpoint graph), computed with Python versions
   that give the same values as the R package on 16 alignments;
 - 27 simple derivations: percent aligned, averages of the _target_ and
   _query_ versions of a statistic, and contrasts between them.

## Candidates

A candidate is a level, one or two vectors and a reducer; none takes a
parameter, and nothing in the list encodes a biological hypothesis.

 - **Level**: the alignments as loaded (2,484 candidates) or coalesced (2,936
   candidates).
 - **Vectors per alignment** (24 or 25): widths on each genome and their
   contrast, distance to the sequence end on each genome, sequence lengths,
   strand relative to the majority strand of the pair of sequences, shift in
   relative position between the genomes, identity, mismatches, gap openings
   and gap columns per alignment column, score per column, share of the
   aligned bases of the sequence, and the gaps and changes found at the two
   flanks.
 - **Vectors per junction** (15 or 19): target gap, change of strand, change
   of _query_ sequence, and the mean and the absolute difference of six or
   eight alignment properties.
 - **Vectors per same-query junction** (5): query gap, rank step on the
   _query_, direction, contrast between target and query gaps, colinearity.

| Reducer family | Candidates | Statistics |
|--------------------------------|-----------:|--------------------------------------------------------|
| Distribution of one vector | 782 | mean, standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis, quartile statistics, Gini, concentration, width-weighted mean and deviation |
| Order along the _target_ genome | 488 | correlation between values 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 positions apart; proportion of local extrema |
| Differences between sequences | 181 | share of the variance between _target_ sequences, _query_ sequences or pairs of sequences |
| Correlation of two vectors | 3,913 | Pearson, rank, width-weighted, within _target_ sequence, between neighbours |
| Table of aligned bases by pair of sequences | 14 | mutual information, conditional entropy, Cramér's V, singular values |
| Permutation of the alignment order | 14 | cycles, fixed points, descents, records, longest increasing subsequence, footrule |
| Patterns of 3 or 4 consecutive alignments | 28 | frequencies and entropies of order patterns and strand patterns |

Two requirements were built in, for well-definedness rather than biology: a
value must not depend on the order of the sequences in the files, nor on the
orientation in which each sequence was written.  On 302 alignments rewritten
with sequences reversed at random, all 5,420 candidates gave the same value
within a relative difference of 2 × 10^-5^.

A candidate is named `<level>.<reducer>.<vector>[~<vector>]`.  The names of
the twelve functions in the screen are:

```{r candidates, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(paste0("`", f$fun, "()`"), paste0("`", f$candidate, "`")),
             col.names = c("Function", "Candidate"))
```

In these names, the level is `raw` (as loaded) or `coa` (coalesced).  The
reducers are `tailw` (tail weight), `bowley` (quartile skewness), `kurt`
(excess kurtosis), `sd` (standard deviation), `pcor` (Pearson correlation),
`rcor` (rank correlation), `wcor` (correlation weighted by alignment width)
and `xcor` (correlation between neighbours).  The vectors are `qstep` (query
gap), `gdiff` (gap contrast), `pdisp` (shift in relative position), `tedge`
and `qedge` (edge distance on the _target_ and on the _query_), `tw` (width on
the _target_), `rstep` (rank step), `dirc` (direction), `tgap` (target gap),
`sdens` (score per alignment column), `gapf` (gap openings per alignment
column) and `bgap` (geometric mean of the target gaps at the two flanks);
`jm_` and `jd_` are the mean and the absolute difference of a vector over the
two alignments of a junction.

## Filters

The largest losses are at definedness, reciprocal agreement and the shuffling
test.  Novelty then leaves 43 candidates, of which 12 are taken.

```{r funnel, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=3, fig.cap="Candidates left after each filter, applied in this order."}
funnel <- data.frame(
  filter = c("All candidates",
             "Defined in at least 95 % of the alignments",
             "Not uniform: 95 % distinct values",
             "Same value however the sequences are written",
             "Reproduced by the reciprocal alignment",
             "Alike for genome pairs that share an ancestor",
             "Departs from shuffles in half of the pairs",
             "Below 0.6 with the existing statistics",
             "Selected: below 0.6 with each other"),
  left = c(5420, 3279, 2836, 2836, 1245, 1218, 197, 43, 12))
funnel$filter <- factor(funnel$filter, levels = rev(funnel$filter))
ggplot(funnel) +
  aes(left, filter) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey65", width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = formatC(left, format = "d", big.mark = ",")),
            hjust = -0.2, size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous("Candidates left", expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  ylab(NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

The shuffling test keeps 16 % of the candidates that reach it: most functions
that are reproducible and structured by phylogeny describe the alignments
themselves, not their arrangement.  The filters are, in the order applied:

 1. **Defined.**  Finite in at least 95 % of the alignments, and in at least
    90 % of the alignments of every clade but one.  The exception is for
    Buchnera, where 62 % of the alignments coalesce into three chains or
    fewer, which leaves coalesced-level candidates undefined.
 2. **Not uniform.**  At least 95 % distinct values; the most frequent value
    in at most 2 % of the alignments.
 3. **Representation.**  Same value after reversing sequences at random and
    renaming them.
 4. **Reciprocal agreement.**  Rank correlation between the value on the
    alignment of _A_ to _B_ and the value on the alignment of _B_ to _A_ with
    _target_ and _query_ exchanged: median over the clades at least 0.9, first
    quartile at least 0.8.
 5. **Ancestor nodes.**  Within each clade, genome pairs that share their last
    common ancestor in a UPGMA tree built on the P distance have more similar
    values than permuted pairs (_z_ of at least 5 over the 16 clades), also
    after removing the rank of the P distance (_z_ of at least 3).
 6. **Shuffling.**  In each genome pair, the order of the alignments along
    both genomes and their strands are shuffled 5 times; each alignment keeps
    its widths and alignment columns.  The value must differ from the shuffles
    by at least 3 standard deviations in at least half of the 955 pairs.
 7. **Novelty**, with a common ceiling of 0.6 on: the absolute rank
    correlation with each of the 192 references (pooled, within clade, and
    each also partial on the P distance); the predictability from all
    references together, fitted on 15 clades and tested on the 16th (ridge
    regression on ranks, then boosted trees for the finalists); the rank
    correlation with the function's own shuffled value.
 8. **Selection.**  Candidates are ranked by the mean percentile of their
    reciprocal agreement and of their node effect after removing the P
    distance.  They are taken in that order unless correlated at 0.6 or more
    with one already taken.

## Settings that were relaxed

Ten functions were asked for first.  Two settings had to be relaxed to reach
them: the ceiling, raised from 0.2 in steps of 0.1, and the share of pairs in
the shuffling test, lowered from three quarters to one half.  The request was
then extended to twelve functions: the same settings give them, and the first
ten are unchanged.  The table gives the number of functions selected, by
ceiling and by share of the genome pairs in which the shuffling test must be
passed.

| Ceiling | 3/4 of the pairs | 1/2 of the pairs |
|--------:|-----------------:|-----------------:|
| 0.2 |  0 |  0 |
| 0.3 |  0 |  1 |
| 0.4 |  0 |  2 |
| 0.5 |  0 |  6 |
| 0.6 |  5 | 12 |
| 0.7 | 10 | 12 |

The share of pairs was lowered before the ceiling was raised, because low
correlation with existing statistics was the explicit request and the share
of pairs is a setting of this screen.  With three quarters of the pairs, a
ceiling of 0.7 gives ten functions and no more; with one half, selection
stops at the twelve asked for.

Eleven of the twelve functions are at the level of the alignments as loaded.
At the coalesced level, 579 candidates pass the first five filters, 10 depart
from shuffled chains, and one stays below 0.6: `mizaru_index()`, ranked 23rd
of the 43 and the eleventh function taken.  The twelfth, `able_index()`, is
ranked 26th.

# Behaviour on the alignments of the screen

The file `MonkeyIndices_values.tsv`, next to the source of this vignette,
gives the value of each function on each alignment of the screen, as computed
by the Python code of the screen, with the clade, the P distance and a number
that identifies the pair of genomes: each pair has two rows, one per
alignment.  The figures and the table of this section are computed from it;
their code is in the source of the vignette.

```{r values}
v <- read.delim("MonkeyIndices_values.tsv")
dim(v)
length(unique(v$pair))
```

```{r long, echo=FALSE}
funs   <- f$fun
clades <- c("Buchnera", "Rickettsiales", "Neisseriales", "Deinococcota", "Nanobdellati",
            "Discoba", "Saccharomycotina", "Pezizomycotina",
            "Apoidea", "Gastropoda", "Bivalvia", "Otomorpha", "Eupercaria",
            "Ovalentaria", "Other_Neoteleostei", "Primates")
group  <- rep(c("Prokaryotes (5 clades)", "Fungi and Discoba (3 clades)", "Animals (8 clades)"),
              c(5, 3, 8))
long <- data.frame(
  clade = factor(v$clade, levels = rev(clades)),
  P     = v$P,
  fun   = factor(rep(funs, each = nrow(v)), levels = funs),
  value = unlist(v[funs], use.names = FALSE))
long$group <- factor(group[match(long$clade, clades)], levels = unique(group))
shuffled <- data.frame(fun = factor(funs, levels = funs), shuffled = f$shuffled)
monkey_theme <- theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major = element_line(linewidth = 0.2),
        strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0))
```

## Clades

Every function separates clades: between 35 % and 85 % of its variance lies
between them.  Buchnera, whose genomes are nearly colinear, has the highest or
the lowest median for 7 functions, and Bivalvia and Rickettsiales for 4 each.

```{r clades, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=7.6, fig.cap="Median (dot) and interquartile range (bar) of each function in each clade.  Each panel has its own scale.  Dashed line: median after shuffling, when it falls within the scale."}
q <- aggregate(value ~ clade + fun, long, quantile, probs = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))
q <- data.frame(q[c("clade", "fun")], q1 = q$value[, 1], med = q$value[, 2], q3 = q$value[, 3])
inside <- shuffled$shuffled >= tapply(q$q1, q$fun, min) &
          shuffled$shuffled <= tapply(q$q3, q$fun, max)
ggplot(q) +
  aes(y = clade) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = shuffled), shuffled[inside, ],
             colour = "grey45", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = q1, xmax = q3), colour = "grey70", linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_point(aes(x = med), size = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ fun, ncol = 4, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_continuous(NULL, n.breaks = 3) +
  scale_y_discrete(NULL, labels = \(x) gsub("_", " ", x)) +
  monkey_theme
```

```{r behaviour, echo=FALSE}
med  <- sapply(funs, \(n) tapply(v[[n]], v$clade, median, na.rm = TRUE))
rhoP <- sapply(funs, \(n) median(sapply(split(v, v$clade), \(d)
          suppressWarnings(cor(d$P, d[[n]], method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs"))),
          na.rm = TRUE))
eta2 <- sapply(funs, \(n) summary(lm(v[[n]] ~ v$clade))$r.squared)
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    paste0("`", funs, "()`"),
    sapply(funs, \(n) sum(is.na(v[[n]]))),
    paste(round(100 * eta2), "%"),
    sprintf("%.2f", rhoP),
    gsub("_", " ", rownames(med)[apply(med, 2, which.max)]),
    gsub("_", " ", rownames(med)[apply(med, 2, which.min)])),
  col.names = c("Function", "Undefined", "Variance between clades",
                "Correlation with P", "Highest clade", "Lowest clade"),
  align = "lrrrll", row.names = FALSE)
```

 - **Undefined**: number of alignments, out of 1,910, where the function
   returns no value.
 - **Variance between clades**: share of the variance of the function that
   lies between the clades.
 - **Correlation with P**: rank correlation with the P distance within a
   clade, median of the 16 clades.

## Divergence

Within clades, the rank correlation with the P distance is weak for ten
functions (between -0.15 and 0.11); it is 0.30 for `albert_index()` and -0.35
for `hanuman_index()`.  Across clades, divergence and kind of organism are
confounded: all the alignments of insects, fishes and primates have a P
distance below 0.27, and 90 % of the alignments of the ten other clades have
one above 0.3.

```{r divergence, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=8.8, fig.cap="Each function against the P distance, one dot per alignment.  Vertical axes cover the 1st to 99th percentiles of each function.  Dashed line: median after shuffling, when it falls within the axis."}
lim  <- sapply(funs, \(n) quantile(v[[n]], c(0.01, 0.99), na.rm = TRUE))
keep <- which(long$value >= lim[1, as.integer(long$fun)] &
              long$value <= lim[2, as.integer(long$fun)])
set.seed(1)  # no group systematically on top
keep <- sample(keep)
inside <- shuffled$shuffled >= lim[1, ] & shuffled$shuffled <= lim[2, ]
ggplot(long[keep, ]) +
  aes(P, value, colour = group) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = shuffled), shuffled[inside, ],
             colour = "grey35", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(size = 0.35, alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ fun, ncol = 3, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(NULL, values = c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a")) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 2.5, alpha = 1))) +
  labs(x = "P distance", y = NULL) +
  monkey_theme +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

# Limits

The twelve functions are sound as computations.  What they mean is open, and
several of the settings that selected them are arbitrary.

 - **Sample.**  Close pairs are few: 4 % of the alignments have a P distance
   below 0.1.  The seed and the kind of organism are confounded: MAM8 for
   prokaryotes and fungi, RY4 for animals and Discoba.  No alignment has more
   than 250 sequences, so the filter of the statistics pipeline of the
   project (the 250 sequences with the most aligned bases) was never applied.
 - **Settings near their limits.**  The shuffling test uses 5 shuffles per
   pair.  `albert_index()`, `mizaru_index()`, `baker_index()` and
   `marcel_index()` pass it in 50.5 %, 50.7 %, 51.1 % and 53.7 % of the pairs,
   for a requirement of 50 %.  `imo_index()` is at 0.59 with the strand
   randomisation index, and `able_index()` at 0.58 with `rafiki_index()`, for
   a ceiling of 0.6.
 - **Excluded by construction.**  623 candidates can not change when
   alignments are shuffled: the distributions of alignment widths, identity
   and gaps, and the correlations between them.  213 of them pass the first
   five filters; they are flagged in the column `free` of the table of metrics
   that the scripts write (`results/metrics_all.tsv`), and can be screened
   separately.
 - **Readings.**  `abu_index()`, `albert_index()`, `rafiki_index()`,
   `hanuman_index()`, `jack_index()` and `able_index()` respond to the share
   of junctions that are not colinear, each in a different way; their largest
   correlations with the synteny, breakpoint and chain statistics are between
   0.53 and 0.57.  They may be partial readouts of colinearity.
 - **Reference set.**  Functions that exist only on development branches of
   _GenomicBreaks_ were not in the references, nor was the inversion distance
   with hurdles.
 - **Run time.**  On 47 alignments holding 2.25 million alignment blocks, each
   function took 2.0 to 3.7 seconds, except `mizaru_index()`, which coalesces
   the alignments first and took 42 seconds (R 4.3.3, Bioconductor 3.18).

The R functions give the same values as the Python code of the screen on
these 47 alignments, drawn from all clades: the largest relative difference is
6 × 10^-8^.  Their values are unchanged by `reverse()` on the _target_, and
change by at most 3 × 10^-7^ with `reverse(query = TRUE)`.

# Reproducing the screen

The code of the screen is distributed with the package, for the record: no
function of the package uses it.

```{r scripts}
list.files(system.file("scripts", "monkey_screen", package = "GenomicBreaks"))
```

It needs Python 3 with _numpy_, _scipy_, _pandas_, _scikit-learn_ and
_PyYAML_.  The run of 2026-11-11 used Python 3.13, two cores and 7 GB of
memory, and took about 2.5 hours of computation.

**Input.**  `extractMonkeySubset.py` selects the genomes and writes one tar
file per clade.  For each clade that has both alignments and up-to-date
statistics, it computes the P distance of every ordered pair from the
`.o2o.matrix.txt` files, builds a UPGMA tree, cuts it in a given number of
clades (2 in the run that was used), picks a given number of genomes (12) and
exports, for every ordered pair of them, the `.blasttabplus.gz`,
`.o2o.matrix.txt`, `.o2o.tsv` and `.yaml` files.  The paths in this script are those of the
project on its computing cluster.  The tar files are unpacked in
`$MONKEY_ROOT/data/monkey/`.

**Steps.**  Set the environment variable `MONKEY_ROOT` to a working directory
that contains `data/monkey/`, and run the scripts in order.  The `mk_*.py`
files are modules.

| Script | Does | Time |
|------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|---------:|
| `01_build_cache.py` | parses the alignments once and applies the filter of the statistics pipeline (250 sequences with the most aligned bases) | 3 min |
| `02_existing.py` | table of the YAML statistics | 1 min |
| `03_validate.py` | checks the loader and the coalescing against the YAML counts and totals | 1 min |
| `04_test_engine.py` | checks the candidate engine on four alignments | 1 min |
| `05_stage1.py` | all candidates on all alignments, as they are and with _target_ and _query_ exchanged | 50 min |
| `06_extras.py` | adds to the reference table the package indices that are not in the YAML files, and simple derivations | 3 min |
| `07_check_existing.R` | values of the R package, to compare with `mk_existing.py` | 1 min |
| `08_metrics.py` | definedness, reciprocal agreement, ancestor-node agreement, correlation with the references | 5 min |
| `09_invariance.py` | same value when sequences are reversed and renamed | 1 min |
| `10_null.py` | all candidates on 5 shuffles of each genome pair | 65 min |
| `11_redundancy.py` | predictability from all references together (ridge, leave one clade out) | 2 min |
| `12_shortlist.py` | joins the metrics (`results/metrics_all.tsv`) | 1 min |
| `13_null_metrics.py` | departure from the shuffles | 1 min |
| `14_select.py 12` | filters, relaxation, selection of the number of functions given as argument (`results/selected.tsv`) | 2 min |
| `15_final.py` | recomputes the selected candidates on every alignment (`results/final_values.tsv`) | 5 min |
| `16_r_check.R` | values of the R functions on a list of alignments, also after `swap()` and `reverse()` | 2 min |
| `17_final_metrics.py` | all metrics of the selected candidates, from the final values | 2 min |
| `18_figure.py` | each selected function against the P distance, as a PDF file | 1 min |
| `19_vignette_tables.py` | the two tables read by this vignette | 1 min |

**Notes.**

 - The values of step 5 were computed before late changes of `mk_engine.py`
   (ties of the majority strand; a zero-variance guard).  The selected
   candidates were recomputed afterwards: one of them, `raw.sd.pdisp`, changed
   by at most 0.13 %.
 - The shuffles of the coalesced level shuffle the coalesced alignments and
   do not coalesce them again.
 - The docstring of `14_select.py` lists the filters and the two settings that
   were relaxed; the header of `mk_engine.py` lists the vectors and the
   reducers.
